title: Compound conditions and logical operators (&&, ||, !)

visuals.title: AND (&&): true only when BOTH sides are true
OR (||): true when AT LEAST ONE side is true
NOT (!): flips true to false and false to true
Compound condition: marks must be between 0 and 100 to be valid

goal: After this you can join two or more conditions with &&, || and !, predict the result with a truth table, write a correct range check, and explain short-circuit evaluation.
warmup: To get your exam roll number slip, the office says: 'You need your fee challan AND your student card.' If you have only one, you do not get the slip. To enter a ground for free, the rule may be: 'Students OR staff.' Either one is enough. And a shop sign says 'NOT open on Sunday.' Real life already uses AND, OR and NOT. C++ uses the same ideas to check more than one thing in a single if.
definition: A compound condition joins two or more simple conditions. C++ has three logical operators. && means AND: true only when both sides are true. || means OR: true when at least one side is true. ! means NOT: it reverses a condition, so true becomes false and false becomes true. The result of every logical operator is a bool, either true or false.
howItWorks: The computer reads a compound condition from left to right and uses the precedence order: ! first, then arithmetic, then relational (< <= > >=), then equality (== !=), then &&, and last ||. So a || b && c means a || (b && c). Use brackets whenever you are unsure. C++ also uses short-circuit evaluation: it stops as soon as the answer is known. In A && B, if A is false, B is never checked. In A || B, if A is true, B is never checked. Run the trace of the second example to see a function that does NOT run because of this.

worked.problem: Prove short-circuit evaluation. Make a function isBig() that prints a message when it runs. Use it on the right side of && and || and see when the message appears.
pseudocode: IF a AND isBig(20) THEN print First (isBig is skipped because a is false)
IF NOT a OR isBig(20) THEN print Second (isBig is skipped because NOT a is true)
IF a OR isBig(20) THEN print Third (isBig must run, because a is false)
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B["a = false"]
  B --> C{"a && isBig(20) ?"}
  C -->|"False (isBig skipped)"| D[/Print After first/]
  C -->|True| X[/Print First/]
  X --> D
  D --> E{"!a || isBig(20) ?"}
  E -->|"True (isBig skipped)"| F[/Print Second/]
  E -->|False| G
  F --> G{"a || isBig(20) ?"}
  G -->|"isBig runs, returns true"| H[/Print Third/]
  G -->|False| I([End])
  H --> I

explanation.text: isBig() checks if n is above 10.
This line is our spy. If we ever see 'isBig runs', the function was called.
Returns true when n is greater than 10.
a is false.
a is false, so a && anything is already false. isBig(20) is never called.
This prints, and there is no 'isBig runs' before it.
!a is true, so true || anything is already true. isBig is skipped again.
a is false, so || cannot decide yet. It must call isBig(20) to find out.

steps.note: main() starts and sets a to false.
false && ... is already false. C++ skips isBig(20) completely.
Because the if was false, we continue here. Notice that isBig did not print anything.

a is false, so C++ must check the right side. It calls isBig(20).
Inside isBig, n is 20. The spy line prints.
20 > 10 is true, so isBig returns true.
false || true is true, so the block runs.

worked.problem: Write a program that reads a year and tells whether it is a leap year. A leap year is divisible by 4 but not by 100, or it is divisible by 400.
pseudocode: IF (year divisible by 4 AND NOT divisible by 100) OR (year divisible by 400) THEN
PRINT year is a leap year
PRINT year is not a leap year
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read year/]
  B --> C{"(year%4==0 && year%100!=0) || year%400==0 ?"}
  C -->|True| D[/Print leap year/]
  C -->|False| E[/Print not a leap year/]
  D --> F([End])
  E --> F

sample.title: Leap year with &&, || and brackets
sample.expectedOutput: Enter year: 1900 is not a leap year.

explanation.text: year stores the year we read.
Reads the year from the keyboard.
year % 4 == 0 means divisible by 4. The && part needs divisible by 4 AND not by 100. The || adds the other way to be a leap year: divisible by 400. Brackets make the grouping clear.
Printed when the whole condition is true.
Printed otherwise. For 1900: 1900 % 4 == 0 is true, but 1900 % 100 != 0 is false, so the left group is false. 1900 % 400 is 300, so the right group is false too.

mistakes.error: It compiles. g++ -Wall only warns 'comparisons like X<=Y<=Z do not have their mathematical meaning'. C++ computes 0 < x first, which gives 1 or 0, then compares that with 10. So for x = 15 it still prints 'in range'.
It compiles with no error, but 6 alone is non-zero, which counts as true. The condition is always true (it printed 'five or six' for x = 15).
It compiles with no error, but no number is below 0 and above 100 at the same time, so it is never true (marks = 120 printed 'never invalid').

examTips: Learn the three truth tables by heart: && is true only for T,T. || is false only for F,F. ! flips the value.
Precedence order: ! then arithmetic then < <= > >= then == != then && then ||. So a || b && c is a || (b && c).
Never write 0 < x < 10. Write x > 0 && x < 10. Examiners love this mistake.
Short-circuit: in A && B, B is skipped when A is false. In A || B, B is skipped when A is true. A function call or ++ on the skipped side does not happen.
If a question asks for 'inside a range' use &&. For 'outside a range' use ||.

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct way to test that x is between 10 and 20?
quiz.explanation: Write each comparison separately and join them with &&.

quiz.prompt: In the condition a || b && c, which part is evaluated as a group first?
quiz.explanation: && has higher precedence than ||, so it means a || (b && c).

quiz.prompt: int n = 0; Which condition is safe and never divides by zero?
quiz.hint: Short-circuit skips the right side when the left is false.
quiz.explanation: When n is 0, n != 0 is false, so && skips 10 / n. With || the division would run when n != 0 is false.
